label: sec:observations-intro
html:
This chapter collects the physical predictions of the Descartes universe and compares them with experimental data. We assume the knot-to-particle mapping and Skein decomposition (Chapter 7), along with the Gröbner--Shirshov reduction engine and Wedderburn mass formula (Chapter 11). We calibrate the substrate parameter q_0 from those constructions. The molecular extension (Chapter 17) builds on this calibrated q_0.

The central result is the substrate consistency window. Multiple independent physical observables (lepton mass ratios, the fine structure constant, proton-to-electron mass ratio, and nuclear binding energies) each determine the substrate parameter q. These determinations agree within a narrow interval q_0 \approx 1.110. We present particle identification conjectures, CODATA comparisons for fundamental masses, beta decay predictions, and nuclear stability patterns. We propose experimental tests including crystal resonance, proton radius, and Breit--Wheeler pair creation.

Every numerical prediction uses \approx (not =) to indicate that values are derived approximations at q_0, not exact identities. We tabulate error terms and percentage deviations from experimental data.

Notation note. We use plain italic m_e, m_p, m_n for the CODATA-measured electron, proton, and neutron masses. We treat these as experimental input. They are distinct from the categorical mass \mathfrak{m}, which denotes the QOU-derived mass via the topological mass formula \mathfrak{m}(K) = \mathrm{Vol}(K)/\hbar_q^{2}. The role of m_e is an external scaling ruler. It fixes the absolute energy scale. All other masses are predicted as ratios \mathfrak{m}(K)/\mathfrak{m}(4_1) \cdot m_e. When a comparison table juxtaposes "QOU prediction" against "CODATA value", both are in MeV. The ratio is dimensionless and substrate-derived. Because m_e sets the MeV scale by fiat (CAL-1), the predictive content of any nucleon or atomic entry is that dimensionless ratio; the MeV figure is the ratio rendered against the m_e unit, not an independent absolute-mass prediction.
